query: For high-entropy alloys intended for extreme environments, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve elevated-temperature mechanical properties? State the intervention without limiting its class, the proposed mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, the temperature and application boundaries under which it should hold, the prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment whose outcome would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing small amounts of Y and Hf dopants into a refractory high-entropy alloy will refine the grain structure through grain boundary pinning and stabilize secondary phases, thereby enhancing elevated-temperature mechanical properties compared to an undoped baseline.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory high-entropy alloy (e.g., a Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni-Al or AlCoCrFeNi2.1 type alloy) produced by methods such as direct energy deposition or laser cladding, exhibiting a predominantly single-phase solid solution with a relatively fine grain size.
generation.intervention: Co-dope the alloy with yttrium (Y) and hafnium (Hf) during powder mixing or deposition so that these dopants are incorporated into the microstructure.
generation.conditions: Test under extreme high-temperature conditions, around 900 °C, and in environments representative of corrosive molten salts (e.g., 75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl), with baseline measurements taken at room temperature for comparison.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundaries and secondary phase precipitates; the dopants are expected to segregate to grain boundaries and form stable precipitates that inhibit grain growth.
generation.mechanism: Y and Hf dopants preferentially segregate to grain boundaries, acting as pinning agents that limit grain coarsening during high-temperature exposure. This refined grain structure, along with potential precipitate strengthening, enhances load transfer and resistance to creep, thereby improving hardness and yield strength at elevated temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Y and Hf co-doped alloy will exhibit increased microhardness and higher yield strength at 900 °C compared to an equivalent undoped high-entropy alloy, with improved thermal stability and a reduced tendency for grain coarsening under extreme conditions.
generation.baseline: Identical refractory high-entropy alloy manufactured under the same deposition conditions but without Y and Hf doping.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold for refractory HEAs operating up to around 900 °C and in corrosive environments akin to molten salt conditions; performance outside these conditions is not addressed.
generation.uncertainty: The magnitude of the improvement and optimal dopant concentrations require further experimental optimization, and the exact balance between dopant benefits and potential adverse effects (e.g., unwanted phase formation) is uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of refractory HEA samples using identical laser cladding or DED processes: one set with Y and Hf co-doping and one set without. Subject both sets to a heat treatment cycle at 900 °C for 10 hours in a corrosive molten salt environment (75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl). Post-treatment, measure microstructure, grain size, and mechanical properties.
measurements: Grain size distribution and phase identification via SEM, EBSD, and XRD
Yield strength via compression or tensile testing
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Y and Hf co-doped alloy does not show a statistically significant improvement in grain refinement, microhardness, and yield strength at 900 °C relative to the undoped alloy, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractBoth crack-free AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) and Y and Hf co-doping AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA (YHf-EHEA) coatings were prepared by laser cladding. The solidification microstructure, thermal stability, and hot corrosion performance of the coatings at 900 °C under 75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl molten salts were investigated. The experimental results showed that the structure of the as-deposited coatings consisted of FCC and BCC/B2 phases. After heat treatment, an Al-rich L12 phase was precipitated in the FCC phase of all coatings. The grain sizes of the EHEA and YHf-EHEA coatings after heat treatment at 900 °C for 10 h increased by 27.5% and 15.7%, respectively, compared to the as-deposited coatings. Meanwhile, after hot corrosion, the spallation areas of the YHf-EHEA and EHEA coatings accounted for 14.98% and 5.67% of the total surface area, respectively. In this study, a Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni-Al RHEA was deposited using DED. The phase diagram and phase fraction of Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni-Al were analyzed for deposition on Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni-Al. For the deposited Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni-Al, powders of each element were mixed to prepare a mixed Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni-Al powder and deposited on Ti-6Al-4V and Inconel 718 substrates. The microstructure and hardness of the deposited Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni-Al were measured. In addition, HAZ and thermal shielding analyses were performed on the deposited Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni-Al. The primary findings of this study are as follows: SEM images and EBSD analysis were used to investigate the microstructure of the deposited Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni-Al. Phase analysis predicted that the BCC B2 phase was 62.2%, the BCC A2 phase was 21.6%, and C14 Laves phase was 16.2%. However, the σ phase was 64.2%, the BCC A2 phase was 28.2%, and the Ti2Ni phase was 7.6% in the deposited Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni-Al.The microstructure of the deposited Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni-Al consisted of a phase not predicted by the phase analysis but showed a microstructure similar to that of Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni-Al annealed after casting. In addition, the deposited Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni-Al exhibited a fine grain size of 1–35 μm.
